title: The Lord's dog
hook: Kabir calls himself the Lord's dog, with a chain round his neck, going where He leads (Kabir salok, ang 1368)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok: I am the worst of all, and its other half, everyone else is good. Today Kabir lowers himself again, this time with a smile.

Early morning, any street. A dog trots ahead of its person, nose down, tail up, stopping at every post. Then a gentle tug on the leash, and the dog turns, without fuss, and goes the other way. It doesn't sulk. It doesn't argue. It knows whose hand is on the other end. Kabir saw that too, and put himself in the picture. In one of his saloks he doesn't call himself a saint, or a seeker, or even a weaver. He gives himself a name, and a collar.
screen: `A DOG TROTS AHEAD.` → `A GENTLE TUG.` → `IT KNOWS WHOSE HAND IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok. Kabir, I am the Lord's dog, and Moti is my name. There's a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go. Moti means pearl. It's a pet's name, the kind you'd call across a yard. So Kabir isn't only lowering himself here. He's also saying he's loved: a dog with a name belongs to someone. Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing, and Kabir chose it anyway, with a little warmth and maybe a little humor. Yesterday he said, I am the worst of all. Today the feeling has shifted, less about faults and more about trust. A dog on a leash isn't ashamed. It's attached. The chain could sound like a prison. But listen to who's holding it, and how Kabir answers: wherever He pulls me, I go. No complaint in it. The chain is what keeps him near. Sikh teachers connect this with hukam, the Divine will, and the Gurus' call to walk in it. Not dragged, but led. There's even relief in it. A dog doesn't have to plan the whole walk; it only has to feel the next tug and follow. Kabir doesn't pretend the leash isn't there. He just knows whose hand it's in.
screen: `I AM THE LORD'S DOG.` · `MOTI: A PEARL, A PET'S NAME.` · `WHEREVER HE PULLS ME, I GO.` · `HUKAM: NOT DRAGGED, BUT LED.` · then, large: `LED BY THE CHAIN.`

segments.voice: Think of a small good nudge you've been feeling and ignoring: call your grandmother, drink some water, apologize, go to bed earlier. Don't plan the whole walk; just feel the next small step and agree to it, breathing easy, like a dog trotting beside someone it trusts. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be your yes.
Moti. The pet's name Kabir gives himself in his salok: a pearl, with a cord around his neck, going wherever the Lord pulls.
Your line: led by the chain. Close enough to feel the next tug. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to speak of hukam, walking in the Divine will with trust rather than resistance.

notes: Salok paraphrased; confirm Ang 1368. The text has 'Ram' (the Lord) and 'jevri' (cord/rope); the index says 'chain'. Script uses 'cord' in the paraphrase and keeps 'chain' in the carry as the index requires. Confirm.
'Moti means pearl' is a word meaning, not an etymology; confirm. 'Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing' is a cultural observation, kept soft; confirm.
Hukam and the call to walk in it (cf. Japji): confirm the connection is fairly drawn.
Gurmukhi ਕੂਤਾ as in the salok, 'KOO-taa': confirm.
